## Proof

**Setup and identifications.** We work over a field (with $g$ finite-dimensional so that $(g \otimes g)^* \cong g^* \otimes g^*$, which the problem implicitly assumes by stating $\delta^*: g^* \otimes g^* \to g^*$). The dual pairing extends naturally: for $\xi \otimes \eta \in g^* \otimes g^*$ and $x \otimes y \in g \otimes g$,
$$\langle \xi \otimes \eta,\; x \otimes y \rangle = \langle \xi, x\rangle \langle \eta, y\rangle,$$
and similarly for triple tensor products.

**Step 1: Compute $(\delta \otimes 1)^*$.** The map $\delta \otimes 1: g \otimes g \to g \otimes g \otimes g$ has dual $(\delta \otimes 1)^*: g^* \otimes g^* \otimes g^* \to g^* \otimes g^*$. For $\xi \otimes \eta \otimes \zeta \in g^* \otimes g^* \otimes g^*$ and $x \otimes y \in g \otimes g$:
$$\langle (\delta \otimes 1)^*(\xi \otimes \eta \otimes \zeta),\; x \otimes y \rangle = \langle \xi \otimes \eta \otimes \zeta,\; \delta(x) \otimes y \rangle.$$
Writing $\delta(x) = \sum_i a_i \otimes b_i$, this equals
$$\sum_i \langle \xi, a_i\rangle \langle \eta, b_i\rangle \langle \zeta, y\rangle = \langle \delta^*(\xi \otimes \eta), x\rangle \langle \zeta, y\rangle = \langle \delta^*(\xi \otimes \eta) \otimes \zeta,\; x \otimes y\rangle.$$
Therefore $(\delta \otimes 1)^* = \delta^* \otimes 1$.

**Step 2: Compute $\text{Alt}^*$.** The alternation map $\text{Alt} = \sum_{\sigma \in S_3} \text{sgn}(\sigma)\,\sigma$ is a linear combination of permutation operators on $g^{\otimes 3}$. For any permutation $\sigma$ and $\xi \otimes \eta \otimes \zeta \in (g^*)^{\otimes 3}$, $x \otimes y \otimes z \in g^{\otimes 3}$:
$$\langle \sigma^*(\xi \otimes \eta \otimes \zeta),\; x \otimes y \otimes z\rangle = \langle \xi \otimes \eta \otimes \zeta,\; \sigma(x \otimes y \otimes z)\rangle = \langle \sigma(\xi \otimes \eta \otimes \zeta),\; x \otimes y \otimes z\rangle,$$
since permuting the tensor factors on either side yields the same product of pairings. Hence $\sigma^* = \sigma$ under the identification, and so $\text{Alt}^* = \text{Alt}$.

**Step 3: Take the dual of the composition.** The map $\text{Alt}(\delta \otimes 1)\delta: g \to g^{\otimes 3}$ is the composition (applied right to left):
$$g \xrightarrow{\delta} g \otimes g \xrightarrow{\delta \otimes 1} g^{\otimes 3} \xrightarrow{\text{Alt}} g^{\otimes 3}.$$
Its dual is the reverse composition of the duals:
$$(\text{Alt}(\delta \otimes 1)\delta)^* = \delta^* \circ (\delta \otimes 1)^* \circ \text{Alt}^* = \delta^* \circ (\delta^* \otimes 1) \circ \text{Alt}.$$
This is precisely the map $\delta^*(\delta^* \otimes 1)\text{Alt}: g^* \otimes g^* \otimes g^* \to g^*$.

**Step 4: Conclude.** If $\text{Alt}(\delta \otimes 1)\delta = 0$, then its dual $(\text{Alt}(\delta \otimes 1)\delta)^* = 0$ (the dual of the zero map is the zero map). By Step 3, this dual is exactly $\delta^*(\delta^* \otimes 1)\text{Alt}$. Therefore:
$$\delta^*(\delta^* \otimes 1)\text{Alt} = 0.$$

**Answer: Yes.** The co-Jacobi-type condition $\text{Alt}(\delta \otimes 1)\delta = 0$ implies $\delta^*(\delta^* \otimes 1)\text{Alt} = 0$, because the latter is precisely the dual of the former, and the dual of a zero map is zero.
